rbmi: Modeling count data

Daniel Sabanés Bové

Source: vignettes/count.Rmd
count.Rmd

Now we’ll walk through how count data can be modeled using the rbmi package. The following sections will cover the necessary steps to prepare your data, draw parameter samples, impute missing values, and pool estimates across multiple imputations. For the statistical method details please see the separate vignette. The runtimes reported below are elapsed times measured when this vignette is built and will vary with the computing environment.

1 The Data

We use the simulated example data set generated with the NM_Simdata2.sas macro by James Roger previously available from the LSHTM website (they host content for DIA SWG on Estimands and Missing Data). The data contain three treatment arms and up to three rows per patient, corresponding to the on-treatment, off-treatment but observed, and post-withdrawal periods.

The simulation was informed by characteristics of the METREO study of mepolizumab in eosinophilic chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, but these are not trial data and the simulated treatment effects should not be interpreted as METREO results. Patients either complete follow-up on treatment, discontinue treatment and remain observed until the end of follow-up, discontinue treatment and remain observed for a time before withdrawing, or discontinue treatment and withdraw immediately. Period 1 represents time on treatment, period 2 observed time off treatment, and period 3 unobserved time after withdrawal. Counts were also simulated for period 3 and retained as the complete-data truth for evaluating the analysis, although they are set to missing in the observed outcome.

library(dplyr)
library(rbmi)

dat_count_raw <- read.csv(
    system.file("extdata", "sim_rogeretal.csv", package = "rbmi")
)
dat_count <- dat_count_raw %>%
    dplyr::select(
        patient,
        period,
        TreatLab,
        OnOff,
        Length,
        BaseCount,
        Observed_Count
    ) %>% 
    mutate(
        patient = factor(patient),
        period = factor(period, levels = 1:3),
        TreatLab = factor(TreatLab, levels = c("Placebo", "100mg", "300mg")),
        OnOff = factor(OnOff, levels = c("On", "Off"))
    ) %>% 
    arrange(patient, period)
head(dat_count)
#>   patient period TreatLab OnOff Length BaseCount Observed_Count
#> 1       1      1  Placebo    On    367         1              2
#> 2       2      1  Placebo    On    360         4              1
#> 3       3      1  Placebo    On    372         5              2
#> 4       4      1  Placebo    On    358         7              3
#> 5       5      1  Placebo    On    370         3              1
#> 6       6      1  Placebo    On    370         3              2

The variables retained for this example are:

  • patient: patient identifier.
  • period: follow-up period (1 = on treatment, 2 = off treatment but observed, and 3 = off treatment and unobserved).
  • TreatLab: randomized treatment group (Placebo, 100mg, or 300mg).
  • OnOff: indicator of whether the patient was on or off treatment during the period.
  • Length: time spent in the period, in days.
  • BaseCount: number of events experienced during the year before the study, used as a baseline covariate.
  • Observed_Count: observed number of events during the period; this is missing for period 3 because that period occurs after withdrawal.

The source data omit periods with zero length. We use expand_locf() to add these rows so that every patient has all three periods. The treatment arm and baseline count are carried forward, while OnOff is derived from the period. Added rows have zero length and a missing observed count.

The period column supplied to draws() must be a factor with no unused levels. Set the levels in the order in which periods should be processed. rbmi keeps the factor’s ordered status and any custom contrasts. To model a continuous trend, include a separate numeric period column as a covariate.

dat_count_filled <- dat_count %>%
    expand_locf(
        patient = levels(dat_count$patient),
        period = levels(dat_count$period),
        vars = c("TreatLab", "BaseCount"),
        group = "patient",
        order = c("patient", "period")
    ) %>% 
    mutate(
        OnOff = factor(
            ifelse(period == "1", "On", "Off"),
            levels = c("On", "Off")
        ),
        Length = ifelse(is.na(Length), 0, Length)
    )

SAS reference results for the models illustrated below were computed with the SAS macros NM_Reg22.sas and NM_Rand13.sas by James H. Roger (2021). Note that these can be downloaded as part of the archive NegMult20210313 here available under “Imputation of Recurrent event data for partial observed off-treatment data” on the DIA Missing Data website. The results are included as a CSV file with the package. We retain the two active-treatment versus placebo contrasts, so they can be compared directly with the pooled rbmi estimates. The assertions below stop vignette precompilation if any relative difference from SAS exceeds 0.005 for rate ratios and confidence limits, or 0.10 for p-values. These tolerances allow for Monte Carlo variation between the two implementations and across computing environments. Comparisons use unrounded results and match contrasts by name. When a comparison fails, inspect the Stan diagnostics before increasing the number of imputations: additional draws from a chain that has not converged do not resolve the discrepancy.

sas_results <- read.csv(
    system.file("extdata", "results.csv", package = "rbmi"),
    check.names = FALSE
) %>%
    dplyr::filter(
        (TreatLab == "100mg" & `_TreatLab` == "Placebo") |
            (TreatLab == "300mg" & `_TreatLab` == "Placebo")
    ) %>%
    dplyr::transmute(
        model = Label,
        comparison = paste(TreatLab, "vs", `_TreatLab`),
        sas_rate_ratio = EXP_Est,
        sas_lower_95 = Low_95PCT,
        sas_upper_95 = Upp_95PCT,
        sas_p_value = Pvalue
    )

check_rate_ratio_results <- function(x, sas_model) {
    expected_comparisons <- c(
        "100mg vs Placebo",
        "300mg vs Placebo"
    )
    sas_subset <- dplyr::filter(sas_results, model == sas_model)
    stopifnot(
        setequal(x$comparison, expected_comparisons),
        nrow(x) == 2,
        all(is.finite(as.matrix(x[, setdiff(names(x), "comparison")]))),
        all(x[[2]] > 0),
        all(x[[3]] < x[[2]]),
        all(x[[2]] < x[[4]]),
        all(x[[5]] >= 0 & x[[5]] <= 1),
        setequal(sas_subset$comparison, expected_comparisons),
        nrow(sas_subset) == 2,
        all(is.finite(as.matrix(
            sas_subset[, setdiff(names(sas_subset), c("model", "comparison"))]
        )))
    )
    # Match contrasts explicitly because SAS and rbmi may order them differently.
    sas_subset <- sas_subset[match(x$comparison, sas_subset$comparison), ]
    statistics <- c("rate_ratio", "lower_95", "upper_95", "p_value")
    relative_tolerance <- c(0.005, 0.005, 0.005, 0.10)
    for (i in seq_along(statistics)) {
        actual <- x[[i + 1]]
        expected <- sas_subset[[paste0("sas_", statistics[i])]]
        difference <- abs(actual - expected)
        failed <- which(difference > relative_tolerance[i] * abs(expected))
        if (length(failed)) {
            stop(
                sprintf(
                    paste0(
                        "SAS comparison failed for %s (%s), %s: ",
                        "rbmi = %.8g, SAS = %.8g, relative tolerance = %g"
                    ),
                    sas_model,
                    x$comparison[failed[1]],
                    statistics[i],
                    actual[failed[1]],
                    expected[failed[1]],
                    relative_tolerance[i]
                ),
                call. = FALSE
            )
        }
    }
    invisible(x)
}

2 Draws

The inputs to the draws() function are now:

  • data: The data frame as prepared above.
  • data_ice: Subject-specific imputation strategies for missing count periods
  • vars: The variables to be used in the model
  • method: Here we can only use method_bayes() for fully Bayesian multiple imputation for our count data
  • outcome (new): The outcome type, which defaults to “continuous”, but here we will choose “count”

For count outcomes, data_ice contains only the subject ID and strategy columns; it has no period or visit column. It does not record an intercurrent-event (ICE) time, and no ICE time is inferred from duration. The strategy assigned to a subject applies to every missing positive-duration period for that subject. Consequently, JR and CR are reference-based assumptions for all of that subject’s missing periods, rather than post-ICE-only assumptions. Use MAR for subjects whose missing periods should retain their randomized-arm trajectory.

2.1 Imputation strategies

Here we just use the same imputation strategy for all patients, but we would also be able to provide different strategies for each patient.

Let’s use the Missing At Random (MAR) strategy for all patients with positive post-withdrawal exposure in period 3. This matches the first model in the “Another case with three periods” analysis, where the period-3 design matrix retains each patient’s randomized treatment arm:

dat_ice <- dat_count_filled %>% 
    filter(period == "3", Length > 0) %>%
    dplyr::select(patient) %>%
    distinct() %>% 
    mutate(
        strategy = "MAR"
    )

2.2 Variables

Next we define the variables to be used in the model.

vars <- set_vars(
    outcome = "Observed_Count",
    subjid = "patient",
    period = "period",
    duration = "Length",
    group = "TreatLab",
    covariates = c("TreatLab * OnOff", "BaseCount")
)

Note that here we can also specify interaction terms in the covariates argument, which will then be included in the draws step model.

2.3 Method

We just use the standard Bayesian method options:

method <- method_bayes(
    n_samples = 1000,
    control = control_bayes(
        warmup = 200,
        thin = 5,
        seed = 1821 # Seed to be used by Stan
    )
)

2.4 Sampling

Finally we can call the draws() function to draw samples from the posterior distribution of the model parameters:

set.seed(987)
drawObj <- draws(
    outcome = "count",
    data = dat_count_filled,
    data_ice = dat_ice,
    vars = vars,
    method = method,
    quiet = TRUE
)

3 Impute

Now we basically just run the imputation:

imputeObj <- impute(drawObj)
imputeObj
#> 
#> Imputation Object
#> -----------------
#> Number of Imputed Datasets: 1000
#> Endpoint Type: count
#> Number of Patients with Positive Duration by Period:
#>     1: 674
#>     2: 58
#>     3: 83
#> References:
#>     Placebo -> Placebo
#>     100mg   -> 100mg
#>     300mg   -> 300mg

4 Analyse

Then the next step is the analysis of the imputed data. We can use a similar negative binomial regression model as above, however here we don’t have anymore the OnOff variable, because we have imputed the post-withdrawal periods. So we just use baseline count as additional covariate, next to the treatment group. The imputed values replace the missing values in the original outcome column. We therefore keep Observed_Count as the outcome name. The analysis function sums this outcome and Length over periods for each patient before fitting the model; it does not require a separate Imputed_Count column.

ana_vars <- set_vars(
    outcome = "Observed_Count",
    subjid = "patient",
    period = "period",
    duration = "Length",
    group = "TreatLab",
    covariates = c("BaseCount")
)
anaObj <- analyse(
    imputeObj,
    neg_bin_regression,
    vars = ana_vars
)

Additive delta adjustments to completed counts are not supported. For count sensitivity analyses, use rate multipliers in count_strategy() when specifying the imputation strategies.

5 Pool

Finally we can pool all regression coefficients across the multiple imputations. Pooling is performed on the log-rate scale using Rubin’s rules, with confidence intervals and p-values based on a t distribution with the pooled degrees of freedom.

poolObj <- pool(
    anaObj,
    conf.level = 0.95,
    alternative = "two.sided"
)
poolObj
#> 
#> Pool Object
#> -----------
#> Number of Results Combined: 1000
#> Method: rubin
#> Rubin df method: barnard-rubin
#> Confidence Level: 0.95
#> Alternative: two.sided
#>

6 Comparison with SAS results

The corresponding SAS results are labelled NM_Reg: Treat*OnOff BaseCount.

rate_ratios_shared <- as.data.frame(poolObj) %>%
    dplyr::filter(parameter %in% c("TreatLab100mg", "TreatLab300mg")) %>%
    dplyr::transmute(
        comparison = dplyr::recode(
            parameter,
            TreatLab100mg = "100mg vs Placebo",
            TreatLab300mg = "300mg vs Placebo"
        ),
        rbmi_rate_ratio = est,
        rbmi_lower_95 = lci,
        rbmi_upper_95 = uci,
        rbmi_p_value = pval
    )
check_rate_ratio_results(
    rate_ratios_shared,
    "NM_Reg: Treat*OnOff BaseCount"
)

dplyr::left_join(
    rate_ratios_shared,
    dplyr::filter(sas_results, model == "NM_Reg: Treat*OnOff BaseCount"),
    by = "comparison"
) %>%
    dplyr::select(-model) %>% 
    dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)))
#>         comparison rbmi_rate_ratio rbmi_lower_95 rbmi_upper_95 rbmi_p_value
#> 1 100mg vs Placebo          0.7651        0.6142        0.9531       0.0169
#> 2 300mg vs Placebo          0.8373        0.6785        1.0334       0.0981
#>   sas_rate_ratio sas_lower_95 sas_upper_95 sas_p_value
#> 1         0.7663       0.6150       0.9548      0.0177
#> 2         0.8382       0.6792       1.0344      0.1000

Runtime: draw 78.08 seconds, impute 23.13 seconds, analyse 84.29 seconds, and pool 0.13 seconds.

7 Additional modeling options

7.1 Separate draw model sampling for each treatment group

The default count model uses one dispersion/frailty parameter across all treatment groups. To estimate a separate parameter for each group, set same_cov = FALSE in method_bayes(). The name is retained for consistency with continuous-outcome models; for count outcomes it controls whether phi is shared between groups.

To make the complete imputation model separate by treatment arm, all fixed effects must also be interacted with treatment. For the example data this is:

vars_by_arm <- set_vars(
    outcome = "Observed_Count",
    subjid = "patient",
    period = "period",
    duration = "Length",
    group = "TreatLab",
    covariates = c(
        "TreatLab:OnOff",
        "TreatLab:BaseCount"
    )
)

method_by_arm <- method_bayes(
    same_cov = FALSE,
    n_samples = 1000,
    control = control_bayes(
        warmup = 200,
        thin = 5,
        seed = 1821
    )
)
set.seed(987)
drawObj_by_arm <- draws(
    outcome = "count",
    data = dat_count_filled,
    data_ice = dat_ice,
    vars = vars_by_arm,
    method = method_by_arm,
    quiet = TRUE
)

This is fitted in one Stan call, but with treatment-specific fixed effects and independent treatment-specific phi parameters the posterior factorizes by arm. It therefore represents the same statistical model as fitting each arm separately, while retaining a single rbmi draws object and the usual downstream workflow.

For MAR imputation, each subject uses the phi for their randomized treatment arm. For JR and CR, the mapped reference arm’s phi is used for the whole subject-level conditional distribution. In particular, JR still calculates the observed-cell means from the subject’s randomized-arm design, but uses the reference-arm phi when conditioning on those observed cells and when drawing the missing cells. JR therefore combines the randomized-arm observed mean trajectory with the reference arm’s frailty distribution; it is not only a design-matrix substitution for missing periods. This distinction disappears with the default shared phi.

7.1.1 Impute

The downstream workflow is unchanged. Setting the seed immediately before impute() makes the conditional negative-binomial draws reproducible.

set.seed(123)
imputeObj_by_arm <- impute(drawObj_by_arm)

7.1.2 Analyse and pool

The treatment-policy analysis still combines all randomized treatment arms and uses the same analysis model as above. Only the imputation model has changed.

anaObj_by_arm <- analyse(
    imputeObj_by_arm,
    neg_bin_regression,
    vars = ana_vars
)
poolObj_by_arm <- pool(
    anaObj_by_arm,
    conf.level = 0.95,
    alternative = "two.sided"
)
poolObj_by_arm
#>

For comparison with implementations that report treatment effects as rate ratios, extract the transformed pooled results:

rate_ratios_by_arm <- as.data.frame(poolObj_by_arm) %>%
    filter(parameter %in% c("TreatLab100mg", "TreatLab300mg")) %>%
    transmute(
        comparison = recode(
            parameter,
            TreatLab100mg = "100mg vs Placebo",
            TreatLab300mg = "300mg vs Placebo"
        ),
        rate_ratio = est,
        lower_95 = lci,
        upper_95 = uci,
        p_value = pval
    )
check_rate_ratio_results(
    rate_ratios_by_arm,
    "NM_Reg: Separate for each Treat."
)
rate_ratios_by_arm
#>         comparison rate_ratio  lower_95  upper_95    p_value
#> 1 100mg vs Placebo  0.7682772 0.6177404 0.9554982 0.01783257
#> 2 300mg vs Placebo  0.8388777 0.6810196 1.0333268 0.09858468

7.1.3 Comparison with SAS results

The corresponding SAS results are labelled NM_Reg: Separate for each Treat..

dplyr::left_join(
    rate_ratios_by_arm %>%
        dplyr::rename(
            rbmi_rate_ratio = rate_ratio,
            rbmi_lower_95 = lower_95,
            rbmi_upper_95 = upper_95,
            rbmi_p_value = p_value
        ),
    dplyr::filter(sas_results, model == "NM_Reg: Separate for each Treat."),
    by = "comparison"
) %>%
    dplyr::select(-model) %>% 
    dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)))

7.2 Treatment interaction terms on all model covariates

This model also gives each treatment arm its own on- and off-treatment rates and baseline-count slope. Unlike the preceding model, all arms are fitted in one model, so they share a single dispersion/frailty parameter. This matches the Separate each Treat. Shared frai model in the SAS reference analysis.

7.2.1 Draw and impute

rbmi adds an intercept and the TreatLab main effect to the requested interactions, so the model formula is ~ 1 + TreatLab + TreatLab:OnOff + TreatLab:BaseCount (printed below). The interactions with TreatLab give each randomized treatment arm a separate coefficient for every covariate; same_cov = TRUE (the default) retains the shared count-model dispersion parameter.

For this comparison we use four chains and 4,000 imputations to reduce Monte Carlo variation in the confidence limits relative to the SAS tolerance.

vars_all_treatment_interactions <- set_vars(
    outcome = "Observed_Count",
    subjid = "patient",
    period = "period",
    duration = "Length",
    group = "TreatLab",
    covariates = c(
        "TreatLab:OnOff",
        "TreatLab:BaseCount"
    )
)
set.seed(987)
drawObj_all_treatment_interactions <- draws(
    outcome = "count",
    data = dat_count_filled,
    data_ice = dat_ice,
    vars = vars_all_treatment_interactions,
    method = method_bayes(
        n_samples = 4000,
        control = control_bayes(
            chains = 4,
            warmup = 500,
            thin = 1,
            seed = 1821
        )
    ),
    quiet = TRUE
)

The treatment-policy analysis model is unchanged: it uses randomized treatment and baseline count, without distinguishing on- and off-treatment periods.

    neg_bin_regression,
    vars = ana_vars
)
poolObj_all_treatment_interactions <- pool(
    anaObj_all_treatment_interactions,
    conf.level = 0.95,
    alternative = "two.sided"
)

The corresponding SAS results are labelled Separate each Treat. Shared frai.

7.3 More complex model which also splits time by season

The preceding models use the original three periods. We can also split those periods into smaller calendar cells and include a recurring seasonal effect in the imputation model. This is a genuinely ragged representation: patients need not contribute the same interval identifiers, and a withdrawn patient can have several missing cells.

The source data include Times1–Times20, one-based event-day offsets within each original period: a value of 1 denotes the first day of that period and a value of Length denotes its last day. There is one non-missing Times value for each event in Observed_Count, with the remaining columns left missing; the simulation allowed at most 20 events per period. The start of a period on the study calendar is StartDate + Lengthsofar, so an event’s calendar day is StartDate + Lengthsofar + TimesN - 1. Although simulated event times also exist for the unobserved third period as part of the complete-data truth, Observed_Count is missing there and the split cell outcomes remain missing.

split_time() uses these offsets to allocate each observed aggregate count to 91-day cells. A fixed width of 91 days reproduces the quarter definition in the SAS example. For other applications, interval can instead be "week", "month", "quarter", or "year"; calendar months, quarters, and years require a Date start variable.

dat_count_season <- dat_count_raw %>%
    mutate(
        patient = factor(patient),
        TreatLab = factor(TreatLab, levels = c("Placebo", "100mg", "300mg")),
        OnOff = factor(OnOff, levels = c("On", "Off")),
        cell_start = StartDate + Lengthsofar
    ) %>%
    split_time(
        start = "cell_start",
        duration = "Length",
        outcome = "Observed_Count",
        event_times = paste0("Times", 1:20),
        interval = 91,
        origin = 0,
        period = "period"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
        Quarter = factor(1 + split_interval %% 4, levels = 1:4)
    )

nrow(dat_count_season)
#> [1] 3518
table(dat_count_season$Quarter)
#> 
#>   1   2   3   4 
#> 892 844 906 876

The split data have 3,518 rows and 24 distinct crossed period/quarter cells. As checks on the restructuring, split durations sum to the original duration, observed cell counts sum to the original observed count, and the 83 withdrawn patients contribute 204 missing positive-duration cells.

season_check <- dat_count_season %>%
    group_by(patient, period) %>%
    summarise(
        split_length = sum(split_duration),
        split_count = if (all(is.na(split_outcome))) {
            NA_integer_
        } else {
            sum(split_outcome)
        },
        original_length = first(Length),
        original_count = first(Observed_Count),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

stopifnot(
    nrow(dat_count_season) == 3518,
    nlevels(dat_count_season$split_period) == 24,
    sum(
        is.na(dat_count_season$split_outcome) &
            dat_count_season$split_duration > 0
    ) == 204,
    n_distinct(
        dat_count_season$patient[is.na(dat_count_season$split_outcome)]
    ) == 83,
    all(season_check$split_length == season_check$original_length),
    all(
        season_check$split_count[season_check$period != 3] ==
            season_check$original_count[season_check$period != 3]
    ),
    all(is.na(season_check$split_count[season_check$period == 3]))
)

The count draw model uses a ragged negative-multinomial likelihood: it accepts one row per observed positive-duration cell and accumulates the cell means and counts by patient. There is no padding to a common set of periods and no fixed upper limit on the number of periods.

We add Quarter to the imputation model. split_period uniquely identifies the original period crossed with the absolute 91-day interval and supplies the within-patient ordering used for sequential imputation.

dat_ice_season <- dat_count_season %>%
    filter(is.na(split_outcome), split_duration > 0) %>%
    distinct(patient) %>%
    mutate(strategy = "MAR")

vars_season <- set_vars(
    outcome = "split_outcome",
    subjid = "patient",
    period = "split_period",
    duration = "split_duration",
    group = "TreatLab",
    covariates = c(
        "TreatLab:OnOff",
        "BaseCount",
        "Quarter"
    )
)
drawObj_season <- draws(
    outcome = "count",
    data = dat_count_season,
    data_ice = dat_ice_season,
    vars = vars_season,
    method = method,
    quiet = TRUE
)

During imputation, missing cells are visited in split_period order. For each patient, a draw conditions first on all observed cells. After each missing-cell draw, its sampled count and fitted mean are added to the conditioning totals before drawing the next cell. With only one missing cell, this reduces exactly to the conditional negative-binomial calculation used by the original three-period implementation.

7.4 Fixed rate model for the active arms

The next controlled-imputation analysis retains the estimated off-treatment rate for placebo, but replaces the model-based period-3 rate for both active arms with a fixed value.

There is an important parameterization detail. count_strategy() offers two scales for fixed_rate:

  • fixed_rate_scale = "rate" (the default): fixed_rate is an event rate per unit of duration, so the unconditional mean of the missing cell is \(\mu_{i3} = L_{i3} \times \text{fixed\_rate}\), the same for every posterior draw and treatment arm.
  • fixed_rate_scale = "lambda": reproduces the SAS macro NM_Rand13.sas, which fixes the value on its negative-multinomial lambda scale. If \(r = \phi^{-1}\) is the negative-multinomial shape parameter, the mean is \(\mu_{i3} = r L_{i3} \times \text{fixed\_rate} = L_{i3} \times \text{fixed\_rate} / \phi\). The implied event rate therefore varies with each posterior draw of \(\phi\) and grows without bound when \(\phi\) is close to zero (nearly Poisson data); impute() warns when this implies rates more than 100 times the model-based rate.

To reproduce the SAS results, we select the SAS scale explicitly. For new analyses, the default rate scale is recommended because the specified value is then an interpretable event rate.

In the joint count model, \(\mu_{i3}\) is the unconditional marginal mean of \(Y_{i3}\). The actual imputation distribution, however, conditions on the observed counts \(y_{i1},y_{i2}\). Given these counts and fitted observed-cell means \(\hat\mu_{i1},\hat\mu_{i2}\), its conditional mean is

\[\mathbb{E}(Y_{i3} \mid y_{i1},y_{i2}) = \frac{r + y_{i1} + y_{i2}} {r + \hat\mu_{i1} + \hat\mu_{i2}}\,\mu_{i3}.\]

For a fixed-rate strategy based on JR or CR, \(r\) is calculated from the mapped reference arm’s phi; under JR this is so even though the fitted observed-cell means in the denominator use the subject’s randomized-arm design.

Controlled count strategies are applied in impute(), after the posterior parameters have been drawn. Each strategy has a base trajectory (MAR, JR, or CR) and an optional transformation of the missing-cell rate. Thus the original drawObj can be reused without refitting the observed-data model.

First, we identify the period-3 withdrawals in the active arms and update only their imputation strategy. Placebo patients retain MAR imputation using the estimated placebo off-treatment rate.

active_period3_strategy <- dat_count_filled %>%
    filter(
        period == "3",
        Length > 0,
        TreatLab != "Placebo"
    ) %>%
    distinct(patient) %>%
    mutate(strategy = "FIXED_LAMBDA")

fixed_lambda_strategies <- get_count_strategies(
    FIXED_LAMBDA = count_strategy(
        base = "MAR",
        fixed_rate = 0.0021,
        fixed_rate_scale = "lambda",
        period = "3"
    )
)
set.seed(123)
imputeObj_fixed_lambda <- impute(
    drawObj,
    update_strategy = active_period3_strategy,
    strategies = fixed_lambda_strategies
)

The treatment-policy analysis and pooling steps are unchanged.

anaObj_fixed_lambda <- analyse(
    imputeObj_fixed_lambda,
    neg_bin_regression,
    vars = ana_vars
)
poolObj_fixed_lambda <- pool(
    anaObj_fixed_lambda,
    conf.level = 0.95,
    alternative = "two.sided"
)
rate_ratios_fixed_lambda <- as.data.frame(poolObj_fixed_lambda) %>%
    filter(parameter %in% c("TreatLab100mg", "TreatLab300mg")) %>%
    transmute(
        comparison = recode(
            parameter,
            TreatLab100mg = "100mg vs Placebo",
            TreatLab300mg = "300mg vs Placebo"
        ),
        rbmi_rate_ratio = est,
        rbmi_lower_95 = lci,
        rbmi_upper_95 = uci,
        rbmi_p_value = pval
    )
check_rate_ratio_results(
    rate_ratios_fixed_lambda,
    "Fixed 0.01 active imputed"
)

left_join(
    rate_ratios_fixed_lambda,
    filter(sas_results, model == "Fixed 0.01 active imputed"),
    by = "comparison"
) %>%
    select(-model) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)))
#>         comparison rbmi_rate_ratio rbmi_lower_95 rbmi_upper_95 rbmi_p_value

7.5 Off-treatment estimate is doubled for the active arms

The same controlled-imputation mechanism can multiply rather than replace the model-based mean. Here the active-arm period-3 mean is twice the corresponding estimated off-treatment mean, while placebo is unchanged:

\[\mu_{i3}^{\text{impute}} = 2\mu_{i3}^{\text{model}}.\]

Only the strategy definition changes. Its base remains MAR, so each active-arm patient retains their randomized arm’s modeled off-treatment trajectory and dispersion parameter before the multiplier is applied.

active_period3_double_strategy <- active_period3_strategy %>%
    mutate(strategy = "DOUBLE_RATE")

double_rate_strategies <- get_count_strategies(
    DOUBLE_RATE = count_strategy(
        base = "MAR",
        rate_multiplier = 2,
        period = "3"
    )
)
set.seed(123)
imputeObj_double_rate <- impute(
    drawObj,
    update_strategy = active_period3_double_strategy,
    strategies = double_rate_strategies
)
anaObj_double_rate <- analyse(
    imputeObj_double_rate,
    neg_bin_regression,
    vars = ana_vars
)
poolObj_double_rate <- pool(
    anaObj_double_rate,
    conf.level = 0.95,
    alternative = "two.sided"
)
rate_ratios_double_rate <- as.data.frame(poolObj_double_rate) %>%
    filter(parameter %in% c("TreatLab100mg", "TreatLab300mg")) %>%
    transmute(
        comparison = recode(
            parameter,
            TreatLab100mg = "100mg vs Placebo",
            TreatLab300mg = "300mg vs Placebo"
        ),
        rbmi_rate_ratio = est,
        rbmi_lower_95 = lci,
        rbmi_upper_95 = uci,
        rbmi_p_value = pval
    )
check_rate_ratio_results(
    rate_ratios_double_rate,
    "Delta Active double rate off"
)

left_join(
    rate_ratios_double_rate,
    filter(sas_results, model == "Delta Active double rate off"),
    by = "comparison"
) %>%
    select(-model) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)))
#>         comparison rbmi_rate_ratio rbmi_lower_95 rbmi_upper_95 rbmi_p_value
